name: Bumchu at Tashiding
when: Feb–Mar, 14th–15th day of the 1st Tibetan month (lunar)
community: Bhutia, Lepcha, Sherpa and Buddhist pilgrims from Sikkim, Nepal and Bhutan
summary: Once a year the lamas of Tashiding open a sealed sacred vase and read the coming year in its water: full means plenty, low means hardship. Pilgrims queue through the night for a few drops.
body: Bumchu means 'sacred vase' in Tibetan, and the ritual at Tashiding Monastery centres on a vase that, by monastery tradition recorded in Wikipedia's article on Tashiding, holds water blessed in the time of Guru Padmasambhava in the 8th century. The vase stays sealed all year. On the night of the 14th day of the first Tibetan month, in February or March, the lamas open it in front of the assembled crowd and inspect the level of the water.

The reading is a forecast for Sikkim. If the vase is filled to the brim, the year will be prosperous; if it is low or empty, hardship or famine may follow. After the reading, some of the holy water is shared out to pilgrims, who carry it home in small bottles, and the vase is sealed again for the next year.

Tashiding stands at about 1,465 m on a heart-shaped hill between the Rathong Chu and the Rangeet, and during Bumchu the narrow road from Legship and Yuksom fills with jeeps from across Sikkim, Darjeeling, Nepal and Bhutan. Stalls, prayers and masked figures fill the courtyard. It is a working religious event, not a show, so dress modestly and follow the lamas' instructions.
tips: Book a room in Yuksom, Pelling or Legship well ahead, because Tashiding has very few beds and fills during Bumchu.
Expect long queues for the water late at night; carry a torch, warm layers and a small clean bottle.
Dates follow the Tibetan lunar calendar and move each year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.a: Bumchu falls on the 14th and 15th days of the first month of the Tibetan calendar, about two weeks after Losar, which places it in February or early March. The vase is usually opened on the night of the 14th. Because the date is lunar, it moves every year; we confirm the exact nights with the monastery calendar when you book.

Lamas open a sacred vase kept sealed for a year and read the water level as a forecast for Sikkim's coming year. Full water means prosperity; low water warns of hardship. Some of the water is then shared with pilgrims, and the vase is sealed again for a year. Prayers and ceremonies run through the day and night around it.

Yes, visitors are welcome if they respect it as a religious event. Dress modestly, remove hats inside shrines, walk clockwise around chortens and do not push into the queue for the holy water. Ask before photographing lamas or rituals, and never use flash inside the temples. Crowds are large, so keep children close.

faqs.q: How do I reach Tashiding for Bumchu?
faqs.a: Tashiding is about 40 km from Pelling via Gyalshing and Legship, roughly 2 hours by car, and about 19 km from Yuksom. Shared jeeps run from Gyalshing and Legship, more often during the festival. A reserved car is easiest for a late-night visit. Roads are crowded on festival days, so leave early and check current status before you travel.

name: Pemayangtse mask dances (Chaam)
when: February, 28th–29th day of the 12th Tibetan month (lunar), just before Losar
community: Bhutia and Lepcha Buddhists, with Nyingma monks of Pemayangtse
summary: On the last two days of the Tibetan year, the monks of Pemayangtse, the senior Nyingma monastery of Sikkim, dance in masks in the courtyard to drive out the old year's obstacles before Losar.
body: Pemayangtse Monastery, at about 2,085 m above Pelling, holds its annual mask dances on the 28th and 29th days of the 12th month of the Tibetan calendar, which falls in February. The dates are given in Wikipedia's article on the monastery. The dances end the Tibetan year: their purpose, as in other Nyingma chaam, is to destroy the obstacles and negative forces gathered over the year so that Losar, the new year, starts clean.

The dancers are monks of Pemayangtse, which by tradition takes only ta-tshang, 'monks of pure lineage'. Wearing heavy brocade costumes and painted masks of protective deities, they move slowly to the sound of long horns, cymbals and drums. The climax is usually the destruction of an effigy representing evil. Families from the surrounding villages come in their best clothes, and many travellers time a Pelling trip around the dances.

February is cold in Pelling, around 2–12 °C, but the mountains are often clear, so the festival pairs well with sunrise views of Kangchenjunga. Rooms in Pelling are cheaper than in October. The monastery remains a place of worship during the dances, and the courtyard space is limited, so arrive early.
tips: Arrive by mid-morning to find a place on the courtyard steps; the dances run for several hours each day.
Ask before photographing monks and never step into the dance area for a closer shot.
Tibetan calendar dates move every year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When are the Pemayangtse mask dances?
faqs.a: They are held on the 28th and 29th days of the 12th month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, just before Losar, which usually means February. In 2026 Losar fell in mid-February, so the dances came a day or two earlier. Dates shift every year; we check the monastery's calendar before confirming a festival trip.

faqs.q: What is the meaning of the Pemayangtse chaam?
faqs.a: Chaam are sacred mask dances performed by monks. At the end of the Tibetan year they symbolise the destruction of obstacles and harmful forces, clearing the way for the new year. Masked figures represent protective deities, and the climax often involves the ritual destruction of an effigy. For the community it is both prayer and celebration.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee to watch the Pemayangtse dances?
faqs.a: Pemayangtse normally charges visitors a small entry fee to the monastery, indicatively ₹20–50, and the courtyard dances are open to the public. Fees can change on festival days. Donations to the monastery are welcome but voluntary. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where should I stay for the Pemayangtse festival?
faqs.a: Pelling is the obvious base, 2 km from the monastery, with rooms for every budget. The Elgin Mount Pandim is a five-minute walk from the monastery gate. February is low season, so rates are lower than in October, but book ahead for the festival nights because local families and pilgrims also travel.

name: Maghe Purne at Khecheopalri Lake
when: Magh full moon, usually Jan–Feb (dates vary; confirm each year)
community: Buddhist and Hindu pilgrims; Lepcha, Bhutia, Limbu and Nepali villagers
summary: On the full moon of Magh, pilgrims from Sikkim, Darjeeling, Nepal and Bhutan gather at the sacred Khecheopalri Lake to pray and float butter lamps on small bamboo rafts across the water.
body: Khecheopalri Lake, at about 1,700 m near Khecheopalri village, is sacred to Buddhists and Hindus and to the Lepcha, who know it as Sho Dzo Sho, 'Oh Lady, sit here', according to Wikipedia's article on the lake. Its biggest gathering is the two-day fair of Maghe Purne, the full moon of the Nepali month of Magh. Pilgrims offer prayers, food and khadas, and float butter lamps on small bamboo rafts across the lake.

Sources disagree on timing. 'Maghe Purne' means the Magh full moon, which falls in January or February, and travel writers describe a full-moon celebration with lamps in that season; some printed guides and Wikipedia place the fair in March–April. We confirm the date with the village each year rather than guess. Another observance, Chho-Tsho, is described in some sources as taking place at the lake in October.

The lake is protected by a 2001 Government of Sikkim notification. Swimming, boating and feeding the fish are not allowed, and a wooden jetty lets visitors reach the water's edge without trampling the shore. During the fair the small car park fills quickly, and walkers come up the old paths from the villages below.
tips: Stay a night in a Khecheopalri village homestay or in Pelling so you reach the lake before the crowds.
Keep to the jetty, do not throw coins or food in the water, and walk clockwise around the prayer wheels.
Sources disagree on the date, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the Khecheopalri Lake festival?
faqs.a: The main gathering is Maghe Purne, the full moon of the Nepali month of Magh, which normally falls in January or February. Some guidebooks and Wikipedia place the fair in March–April, so sources conflict. We confirm the date locally every year before planning a festival visit. Check current status before you travel.

Buddhists link it with Guru Padmasambhava and the goddess Tara, and Hindus also revere it; it is often called a wish-fulfilling lake. Lepcha tradition, as recorded in Wikipedia's article, tells of conch shells falling from the sky and a spring rising to form the lake, which became home to a protective goddess.

faqs.q: Are there rules at Khecheopalri Lake?
faqs.a: Yes. The lake is protected by a 2001 state notification. Swimming, boating, fishing and feeding fish are not permitted, and visitors reach the water by a wooden jetty. Remove shoes where signs ask, keep voices low and do not leave litter. A small entry or parking fee may apply.

faqs.q: How far is Khecheopalri Lake from Pelling?
faqs.a: About 30 km, roughly 1.5 hours by car on a branch road off the Pelling–Yuksom route. A reserved car from Pelling for the lake alone costs indicatively ₹2,000–2,800, and most travellers combine it with the waterfalls and Yuksom on a full day for ₹3,500–5,000 per car.
